questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.**

I cannot understand __that you__ are trying to say.
questions.solution:
The correct answer** 'what you'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A** noun clause** functions as **a noun** in a sentence.
 
• It follows a** linking or copular verb** to **describe or modify the subject** of a sentence.
 
• Unlike **Noun phrases**, **noun clauses** contain **both a subject and a verb**.
 
 
• For example: Do you know **what time it is**?
 
 
 
• In the example given above the **bolded noun clauses** are **dependent clauses.**
 
• In the given sentence **'that you are trying to say'** is a **noun clause**.
 
• In this sentence, the most appropriate **pronoun** will be '**what**' instead of '**that**' because '**understand**' does **not** take a **'that-clause.'**
 
• We can use '**what**' as a **pronoun** to mean **'the thing that'**.
 
• Hence,** option 2** is the **correct answer.**

 

**The correct sentence:**__ *I cannot understand **what you** are trying to say.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• A **noun clause** can be used as the **subject**, **direct object, indirect object, object of a preposition, subject complement, or appositive**.

 
 
• Example:
 
 
• Subject: **What I had forgotten** was that I had a test today.
 
• Direct Object: You must choose **which flavor of ice cream you want. **
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/51867102c7c2f369f6e29d2efe025e3b3367c68261ec20262828d84ca5c8f854.png] **Hinglish__**

__
 
• **Noun clause** वाक्य में **संज्ञा** के रूप में कार्य करता है।
 
• यह एक वाक्य के विषय का वर्णन करने या संशोधित करने के लिए एक **linking or copular verb** का अनुसरण करता है।
 
• **Noun phrases** के विपरीत,** noun clauses** में एक **subject** और एक **verb** दोनों होते हैं।
 
 
• उदाहरण: Do you know what time it is?
 
 
 
• ऊपर दिए गए उदाहरण में bold हिस्सा **noun clause dependent clause** हैं।
 
• दिए गए वाक्य में 'that you are trying to say' एक** noun clause **है।
 
• इस वाक्य में सबसे उपयुक्त **pronoun 'what'** होगा क्योंकि '**understanding**' शब्द '**that-clause' **नहीं लेता है।
 
• हम '**what**' का उपयोग **pronoun** के रूप में **'the thing that'** कहने के लिए कर सकते हैं।
 
• अतः **विकल्प 2 **सही उत्तर है।
 
• एक **noun clause** का उपयोग subject, direct object, indirect object, object of a preposition, subject complement, or appositive के रूप में किया जा सकता है।
 
 
• उदाहरण: 
 
 
• **Subject**__: What I had forgotten was that I had a test today.
 
• __**Direct Object:**__ You must choose which flavor of ice cream you want. 
 
 
 
 

 

__**सही वाक्य:**__ *I cannot understand what you are trying to say.*

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

She has gained a lot of fame but still she is __very realistic and sensible__.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is “**down to earth”.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__ **

 
• "Down to earth" is a common idiom meaning being humble, realistic, and sensible, despite any external circumstances such as fame or success.
 
• The other options, "down to it", "down to bottom", and "down to drown", do not convey this sense of humility and practical sense in the same way or are not recognized idiomatic expressions.
 
• "Down to earth" reflects the individual's grounded nature and ability to remain connected to reality despite potential distractions or changes in status.

Hence, the correct answer is ‘**Option 1**’

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.

The Prime Minister as well as his ministers __want__ peace in the country.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'wants'.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• The error lies incorrect usage of the verb 'want'.
 
• Let's take a look at the phrase 'as well as' it means 'in addition' and is used as a conjunction here in this sentence which is connecting two nouns i.e. 'Prime minister and 'his ministers'.
 
• When 'as well as' is used as a conjunction in the sentence, the verb of the sentence agrees with the first noun of the sentence.
 
• Example: 
 
 
• Jack as well as his friends was invited to the party.
 
 
 
• Thus, 'wants' will be used in place of 'want'.

Correct sentence: __*The Prime Minister as well as his ministers **wants** peace in the country. *

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 

 

 
• Conjunction: a word used to connect clauses or sentences or to coordinate words in the same clause.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No improvement’.**

For the last two years Shweta __has being__ diligently working with Rohingya refugees to create colourful table mats using their local weaving techniques.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'has been'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The usage of **'being'** is wrong in the given sentence.
 
• The given sentence is in the** present perfect continuous tense** and **'has been'** is used in the present perfect continuous tense.
 
 
• **E.g.** Girish **has been** working in this company for two years.
 
 
 
• According to the rule and example that are given above, **'has been' **will be used in the **underlined part** of the sentence.

 ​

**Correct Sentence__:** *For the last two years Shweta **has been** diligently working with Rohingya refugees to create colourful table mats using their local weaving techniques.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **The present perfect continuous tense** shows that something started in the past and is continuing at the present time.
 
• The present perfect continuous is formed using the construction **"has/have been + v1 + ing + for/ since + time".**
 
 
• **E.g.** we **have been living** in this house **since **2007.
 
 
 
• **Usage of 'since' and 'for':**
 
 
• **Since** is used for a point of time. 
 
 
• Since Monday, since, 2002, since, last year.
 
 
 
• **For** is used for a period of time.
 
 
• For the last two years, for the last 3 weeks

questions.question:
Select the appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed word in the following sentence to make it grammatically correct.

The grapes taste __(__sweetest__).__.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**sweet**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• The verb "**taste**" in this sentence is a linking verb. Linking verbs connect the subject to a word or phrase that describes or identifies the subject.
 
• When a linking verb is used, it should be followed by an adjective that describes the subject, not an adverb. The adjective tells us about the state or quality of the subject (the grapes).
 
• "**Sweet**" is an adjective in its positive degree.
 
• "**Sweetest**" is the superlative degree of the adjective, used when comparing three or more things. The sentence is not making a comparison, nor is it implying that these grapes are the sweetest among all grapes. It's simply describing their taste.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

Complete Sentence: *"The grapes taste sweet__."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 

 
• **Option 1: "more sweeter"** – This is grammatically incorrect. "Sweeter" is already the comparative form; adding "more" makes it a double comparative.
 
• **Option 2: "sweeter"** – This is the comparative degree, used when comparing two things (e.g., "These grapes taste sweeter than those"). The original sentence doesn't imply a comparison.
 
• **Option 4: "most sweeter"** – This is also grammatically incorrect, being a double comparative with the superlative form.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

The management Is not __beware of__ this fact.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **aware of**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence uses the phrase "**not beware of**" which is incorrect grammar.
 
• "**Beware**" means to be cautious or wary of something, while "**aware**" means having knowledge or understanding of something.
 
• Therefore, the correct phrase should be "**aware of**" indicating that the management should have knowledge of the fact.
 
• The sentence should be written as: *The management is not aware of this fact.*

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 1**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• "**awaking to**" suggests that the management is just starting to become aware of the fact, which is not necessarily implied in the original sentence.
 
• "**beware to**" is not a correct phrase in English. It should be either "beware of" or "be aware of".
 
• "**watchful with**" suggests that the management is being cautious about something, but does not necessarily indicate knowledge of a fact.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.**

Either the bear or the lion __have escaped from__ the zoo.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** 'has escaped from'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is grammatically incorrect.
 
• Here,** 'has escaped from' **should be used instead of** 'have escaped from'.**
 
• We know that if two subjects are connected with 'neither...nor', 'either...or', 'not only...but also', 'or', etc. then the verb should be used according to the nearest subject of the sentence. 
 
• *Example:*
 
 
• *Either Rohit or Rakesh **have** come. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/b91b169c9a6aba309887b5e1410c56688829831001bc1448ed23f1bec5eca1d8.png] *
 
• *Either Rohit or Rakesh **has** come. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/69a779acc017790d2eea790cc9122762921b180090c4a6901b9133fe30db56bd.png] *
 
 
 
• In the given sentence the nearest subject is 'the lion' which is singular. Hence, a singular helping verb should be used.
 
• Therefore, as per the points mentioned above, we find that the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Correct Sentence:__ *Either the bear or the lion has escaped from the zoo.*

questions.question:
In the following sentence the underlined part contains an error. Alternatives to the underlined part are given as options. Select the correct alternative.

The new almirah is__ big__ than this one.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary issue in the sentence is the incorrect comparative form of the adjective "**big**."
 
• Comparative adjectives are used to compare differences between the two objects they modify (larger, smaller, faster, higher).
 
• The correct comparative form of "**big**" is "**bigger**."
 
• Thus, the sentence should be corrected to "**bigger than this one**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The new almirah is **bigger than this one**."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: "more big"** is incorrect because "big" is a one-syllable adjective, and for one-syllable adjectives, we add "-er" to make the comparative form.
 
• **Option 3: "biggest"** is incorrect because "biggest" is the superlative form, used to compare more than two items or people.
 
• **Option 4: "more bigger"** is incorrect because it is a double comparative, which is grammatically incorrect.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment. If no substitution is required select 'No substitution'

__If I would have a degree __from the university, I would get a good job.

options.text: If I am having the degree
When I will have a degree

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **If I had a degree**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase "If I had a degree" is an example of a **conditional statement **in the **past tense**. It expresses a hypothetical situation or a condition that is contrary to reality. In this case, the speaker is saying that if they had a degree, they believe that they would have a better chance of getting a good job. However, since the speaker does not currently have a degree, it implies that they do not currently have a good job or may have limited job opportunities.
 
• This type of conditional statement is known as a **second conditional** or **Type 2 conditional**, which is used to talk about hypothetical or unlikely situations in the present or future.
 
• The incident that happens first or was supposed to happen first takes a **past tense (V2 form of verb)** in the ‘If’ clause when **‘would/could/should + V1’** is present in the **main clause** (result).
 
 
• For example: If I had a bike, I would reach on time.
 
 
 
• Similarly, in this context,** 'had'** (V2) should be in the 'If' clause because **'would + V1' **(would get) is in the main clause.
 
• Hence, 'If I had a degree' is the correct set of words that must substitute the underlined segment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: ***If I had a degree **__from the university, I would get a good job.*

questions.question:

Kranthi loves to swim at the local swimming pool __in order that relieve__ his work stress.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** 'in order to relieve'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The underlined part in the given sentence is grammatically incorrect.
 
• Here,** 'in order to relieve' **should be used instead of** 'in order that relieve'.**
 
• The phrase** 'in order that' **is used to introduce the purpose or the reason for something. It is followed by a clause that explains the **purpose**.
 
• In the given sentence, the purpose of Kranthi swimming at the local swimming pool is to relieve his work stress. So, we need a phrase that can convey the purpose. **Option 4)** **'in order to relieve' **correctly conveys the purpose of Kranthi swimming at the local swimming pool.
 
• Let's see why other options are incorrect:
 
 
• **Option 1) 'in order which'** is incorrect as '**which**' cannot be used to introduce the purpose of something.
 
• **Option 3) 'in order as to relieve' **is grammatically incorrect as the phrase **'in order as to'** is not used in **English**.
 
 
 
• Therefore, **option 4)** is the correct answer.

**Correct Sentence:__** *Krathi loves to swing at the local swimming pool **in order to relieve** his work stress.*

questions.question:

France is a __largest__ country.
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

• "**A**" should be followed by an adjective, not a superlative form.
 
• The word "**largest**" is a superlative and should usually be preceded by "**the**," not "**a**."
 
• The correct form should be "**France is a large country**," using the simple adjective "**large**" instead of the superlative.

Therefore, the correct answer is ‘**Option 4**’.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *France is a **large__** country.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

• "**Was**" is used to describe a state of being or a condition in the past.

A fire broke out in a slum cluster in the capital yesterday **__for short circuit at the overhanging wires.__**

options.text: for short circuit in the the overhanging wires.
due to short circuit in the overhanging wires.
due to short circuiting on the overhanging wires.

questions.solution:
The sentence **mentions an incident and also the reason behind that incident.**

From the given options, the correct way of illustrating a reason is by using **due to** in that sentence. This makes **option 1** wrong.

Now, i**n option 3,** short-circuiting is mentioned which is wrong because short-circuit itself is a Process and the reason for the fire breaking out. We don't have to use continuous ('ing') form there. Also, short-circuiting **on** the wires is wrong, it happened **in** (i.e. inside) the wires. So, **option 3 i**s wrong. 

Hence, **option 2 is the correct answer.**
